The comparison matters because it separates the presence of the practice from the quality of its implementation. A second group received the same amount of time and material support, yet its members were not given a common standard for checking progress. Their results changed little, suggesting that resources alone did not explain the difference. Researchers therefore described the outcome as conditional rather than automatic. This distinction protects the argument from a common logical error: evidence that something can work does not prove that it always works. It also explains why a failed attempt does not necessarily show that the underlying idea has no value. For analysis, the central variables can be classified as the activity itself, the surrounding support, and the measure used to define success. The first identifies what participants did, the second describes the context, and the third determines which changes count as meaningful. When these categories are confused, a reader may attribute an effect to the most visible feature even though a less visible condition produced it. By contrast, careful comparison asks which factor changed, which remained stable, and which alternative explanation is still plausible. The reasoning resembles a scientific process in which an initial hypothesis is revised after evidence reveals an unexpected limitation. Such revision is not a weakness; it converts a broad assertion into a more accurate and useful explanation. The practical implication is that decision makers should test a modest version, record outcomes, and adjust the plan before expanding it. This sequence creates evidence that is relevant to the local setting instead of borrowing certainty from a different population.
